questions.enonce_markdown:
Saul's experience on the Damascus road was very central. Discuss his challenges under Ananias the believer and his rigid resistance to his testimony.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Saul's encounter with the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:1-19; see also 22:3-21 and 26:9-20) is central to Acts and to the history of the Church. The question can be read as asking about the challenges that Saul faced in his relationship with Ananias and with the Christian community, and about the resistance to his testimony. The text is ambiguous here, so the answer treats both the challenges that Saul faced and the reluctance of those who first received him.

**1. The experience itself.** Saul, a zealous Pharisee, was on his way to Damascus with letters from the high priest to arrest followers of "the Way". A light from heaven flashed around him, he fell to the ground and heard a voice: "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" The voice identified itself as Jesus, whom he was persecuting (9:3-5). Saul was left blind for three days, and he neither ate nor drank (9:8-9). This is central because it reversed his direction and led to his call as the apostle to the Gentiles.

**2. Challenges under Ananias.**
- *Dependence and humility.* Saul entered Damascus blind, led by the hand, and he had to wait in prayer for a stranger to come to him (9:8-11). The proud persecutor had to receive help from a disciple of those he came to arrest.
- *Ananias' reluctance.* The Lord told Ananias in a vision to go to Saul, but Ananias objected that he had heard from many about the harm Saul had done to the believers in Jerusalem and that he had authority to bind those who call on the Lord's name (9:13-14). The Lord insisted that Saul was "an instrument whom I have chosen" to carry his name before Gentiles, kings and the people of Israel, and that he would suffer for it (9:15-16). Ananias then obeyed and greeted him as "Brother Saul" (9:17).
- *Healing and baptism.* Ananias laid his hands on Saul, "something like scales" fell from his eyes, he regained his sight, and was baptised and ate (9:17-19). He thus entered the Church through the ministry of an ordinary believer.

**3. Resistance to his testimony.**
- Almost at once Saul preached in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God, and the hearers were amazed because he had come to arrest the believers (9:20-21).
- Jews in Damascus plotted to kill him, and the disciples helped him to escape at night in a basket through an opening in the wall (9:23-25).
- In Jerusalem the disciples were afraid of him and did not believe he was a disciple until Barnabas brought him to the apostles and told them of his conversion (9:26-27).
- Hellenists whom he debated also tried to kill him (9:29).

**4. Assessment.** Saul's difficulties came from two directions: his former friends turned against him as a traitor, while the Christians doubted that the persecutor had really changed. His own personal resistance was ended by the encounter itself, and Acts shows him as obedient to the vision. The resistance he afterwards met reveals the cost of his testimony, as the Lord had said.

**Conclusion.** The Damascus road experience was central because it turned a persecutor into an apostle. His relationship with Ananias showed the humility required of him and the reluctance of the community to trust him, and the opposition that followed fulfilled the words that he would suffer for the name of Jesus.
